Global macroeconomic shock and the downward trend of precious metals. The global precious metals market has drawn a dramatic V-shaped curve over the past week, reflecting the extreme sentiment of investors in the face of landmark monetary policy decisions. Opening the trading session on Monday (June 22), the spot gold price remained stable around $4,160 per ounce. Capitalizing on the initial safe-haven demand, gold quickly established its highest point of the week on June 23 at $4,220.82 per ounce. The real storm hit when the Fed delivered a hawkish message at its Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. While the decision to keep the federal funds rate unchanged at 3.50%-3.75% was not unexpected, the complete removal of dovish language from the official statement sent shockwaves through the stock market. Furthermore, policymakers have sharply revised their forecast for average personal consumption expenditure (PCE) inflation in 2026 upwards to 3.6%. The May PCE report, released this week, also confirmed a 4.1% year-on-year increase. These telling figures reinforce the scenario of monetary tightening, dashing hopes of an early interest rate cut. The direct consequence of this policy was the strong rise of the US dollar. The USD Index (DXY) surged to 101.71 points – its highest level in 52 weeks. A high-value USD combined with an attractive risk-free yield environment created enormous opportunity costs for holding precious metals. Speculative capital immediately fled, triggering a wave of automatic stop-loss orders from algorithmic trading funds. The global precious metals market has drawn a dramatic V-shaped curve over the past week. On June 24th and 25th, spot gold prices plummeted. The precious metal broke through crucial psychological support levels of $4,100 and $4,000 per ounce, hitting a weekly low of $3,959.38 per ounce. From its peak earlier in the week, gold had lost over $260 per ounce in just 48 hours. This harsh high-interest rate environment also led UBS to lower its 2026 gold price forecast from $5,900 to $5,500 per ounce. Not only in Western markets, but physical demand in Asia is also showing signs of weakening. In India , the increase in gold import tax to 15% has significantly reduced purchasing power, while in China, the premium between domestic and international gold prices is rapidly narrowing. By the end of the week, as negotiations in Geneva collapsed, coupled with Iran 's threat to re-blockade the Strait of Hormuz, bargain-hunting money poured into safe havens. This technical bargain-hunting demand became a lifeline, driving gold prices up sharply by $63/ounce, closing the week (June 28) around $4,088.60 - $4,090.60/ounce. Regarding price prospects, the divergence among international financial institutions this week is sharper than ever. Goldman Sachs lowered its year-end target from $5,400 to $4,900 per ounce, although it remains optimistic in the medium term. ING cut its forecast even more sharply: $4,300 per ounce in the third quarter and $4,600 per ounce in the fourth quarter of 2026. Sean Lusk, Director of Commercial Risk Management at Walsh Trading, warned that if US economic data continues to align with the Fed's trend, gold could potentially retreat to the $3,700-$3,800 per ounce range – but he also stressed that this would be a "large buying opportunity" as long-term demand returns.
